title: The Educated Barbarian: Meditations analysis (part. 20)
summary: Part 20 of his Meditations commentary, covering self-determined morality, obeying your own nature, death and cosmic scale, a king's duty to do good and receive reproach, men and destiny, cycles of history, and the danger of comparing yourself to people with better physiques.
claims: Morality pushed on you from outside, rather than thought out yourself, is improper; endless debate over good and evil is pseudo-intellectualism, so live by your own principles
Marcus's 'obey god' means obeying your nature, the source, which in reality means obeying yourself
Law and culture are byproducts of human biology, an arm of nature rather than a force that dominates it
Death is disappearance whether or not life has a purpose; seeing life at a cosmic scale removes the fear of death, but must not slide into nihilism
He believes humans are superior to animals
A king's role is to do good and receive reproach; leaders who stop hearing criticism stop working for their people, which is why tyrannies fail
Men are far more preoccupied with destiny and violent death than women; he has a rehearsed plan for a home intrusion, including where his weapons are
Women have a stronger sense of self-preservation; he suspects men in serious relationships have fewer fatal accidents, as feminine and masculine energies balance each other
History repeats in patterns, and victors rewrite history to look righteous
YouTube fitness presents a lean, muscular body as the holy grail; through the halo effect people assume a good physique means a person has every other quality
Comparison is the thief of joy; there is no point comparing yourself with others unless you compete with them directly, which never happens on YouTube fitness
